chunks.text:
About Brian / Overview
Brian Zhou Liu (goes by Brian Liu) is a data science student at UC San Diego. He loves tinkering with data, software, and research. You can find him building hackathon projects, training models, or exploring San Diego in the sun.

About Brian / Education
University of California, San Diego (La Jolla, CA). Started September 2024 after graduating from Great Neck South High School in June 2024; a junior in the 2026-27 school year. B.S. in Data Science with an AI & ML specialization. GPA 3.95/4.00. Expected graduation June 2028.

chunks.heading: Background
chunks.text:
About Brian / Background
From Long Island, New York; lived in Great Neck and attended Great Neck South High School, which has a dedicated research program (statistics, paper writing, experiment design). Brian applied in 8th grade and started research over quarantine; his first project (from 9th grade) was a vision model classifying knee injuries from MRI scans. About Brian / Why data science
Brian did a lot of AI research in high school and saw data science as the closest major. Computer science felt too technical; he prefers the creative end: applying computing to real-world problems and brainstorming solutions.

chunks.heading: Q-Lab, UC San Diego (Research Intern, Jan 2026 to present)
chunks.text:
Brian's experience / Q-Lab, UC San Diego (Research Intern, Jan 2026 to present)
Research Intern under Prof. Lianhui Qin in La Jolla, CA. Building and evaluating AI systems for scientific simulation and single-cell forecasting. Co-developed SIGA, a Claude Code adapter that configures scientific simulators; built its ChromaDB retrieval layer, MCP XML validator, and plugin framework, and co-authored the paper (accepted as a NeurIPS 2026 poster) (https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.09774). Led a 30-task OpenFOAM transfer study; SIGA's best configuration scored 0.870 accuracy with 30/30 complete cases. On harder held-out GEOS tasks, SIGA raised accuracy by 9.6% from 0.720 to 0.789 and reduced run-to-run standard deviation by about 16x. Curated CellShift, a seven-dataset benchmark testing whether single-cell temporal models generalize to cell fates, lineages and starting populations excluded from training, and conceptualized the experiment (submitted to ICLR 2027; colleagues mostly ran the models). See the CellShift project entry.

chunks.heading: CellShift (2026, Q-Lab, submitted to ICLR 2027)
chunks.text:
Brian's projects / CellShift (2026, Q-Lab, submitted to ICLR 2027)
A benchmark testing whether single-cell temporal models generalize to unseen biology. Brian curated the benchmark and conceptualized the experiment; his colleagues mostly ran the models. The paper is under double-blind review at ICLR 2027, so it is not public yet.
The problem: single-cell RNA sequencing destroys the cell, so time courses are only snapshots of different cells. Models like PRESCIENT, scNODE and CellTempo try to predict gene expression at unobserved times (forecasting later time points, or interpolating between them). But existing benchmarks hold out time points inside cell types and conditions the model already saw in training, so a good score may just mean the model recalls familiar biology.
What CellShift does: seven time-course datasets (blood development, reprogramming, embryogenesis; including LARRY, CellTag, Schiebinger, Pijuan-Sala, Farrell and Moon), with three carrying tasks that hold out cell fates, a lineage or a starting population. One shared evaluator scores everything: statistical baselines, neural dynamics models, pretrained temporal models and language-model agents, and every result is tagged with how much information the method had access to. Lineage-traced data is split by clone.
Findings: on the whole day-6 population of lineage-traced blood development, PRESCIENT and a population-time MLP beat simple copy baselines. But on held-out fates, no fitted model without access to target-day cells beats copying the latest observed snapshot by more than 5%. Simple copy baselines are strong across the benchmark, a low average error can hide an unrealistic predicted population, and LLM agents that pick among a fixed set of numerical tools do about as well as a selector with no language model. Takeaway: current models haven't yet learned dynamics that transfer to unseen cell fates.

chunks.heading: FlashMath (2026, independent project)
chunks.text:
Brian's projects / FlashMath (2026, independent project)
AI-assisted math study desktop app. Built with Tauri, Rust, React, and TypeScript. A cross-platform study app with local persistence, screenshot and PDF ingestion, LaTeX rendering, provider-agnostic AI OCR, and an exam-aware version of the SM-2 review algorithm. Code: https://github.com/brianzliu/FlashMath

chunks.text:
Brian's projects / Blueprint (Jan 2026, NexHacks, 1st place DevTools, 3rd place Token Company, Best Use of Gemini API)
Codebase summarization and vulnerability detection. Built with TypeScript, React Flow, D3.js, AST parsing, Gemini, parallel AI agents, and bear-1 token compression. A VS Code extension that extracts repository structure, maps file dependencies, summarizes code at multiple levels, and flags security risks. Tested on repositories as large as MongoDB. Devpost: https://devpost.com/software/unnamed-pzmyes. Demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tadmUgGUch0

chunks.heading: PillSnap (Apr 2025, UCSD DiamondHacks, Best Use of Auth0)
chunks.text:
Brian's projects / PillSnap (Apr 2025, UCSD DiamondHacks, Best Use of Auth0)
AI-powered pill identifier. Built with Gemini, Vertex AI, the FDA API, Cloud Run, and Vercel. A pill-identification app that combines image descriptions with FDA data, saves medication details, and surfaces drug and food interaction warnings. Devpost: https://devpost.com/software/pill-snap

chunks.heading: Low-Cost Blind Navigation Apparatus (Sep 2022 to Feb 2023, independent research)
chunks.text:
Brian's projects / Low-Cost Blind Navigation Apparatus (Sep 2022 to Feb 2023, independent research)
Wearable computer-vision navigation aid. Built with Python, OpenCV, YOLOv4-tiny, and a Raspberry Pi. A Raspberry Pi head-worn navigation system with real-time audio feedback. Its object detector reached 87.34% mAP while reducing hardware cost by about 90% against commercial alternatives.
